passages.t: Seek the LORD, all you humble
passages.happening:
‘Gather yourselves, gather together, O shameful nation’ (verse 1), before the decree takes effect and the day passes like chaff, before the LORD's burning anger comes (verse 2).

‘Seek the LORD, all you humble of the earth who carry out His justice. Seek righteousness; seek humility. Perhaps you will be sheltered on the day of the LORD’s anger’ (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
Chaff was the light husk blown away when grain was tossed into the wind on the threshing floor. The day of judgment will come as fast as chaff flies.

Verse 3 is the bridge of the whole book. Between the sweeping judgment of chapter 1 and the song of chapter 3 stands this call to the humble, those who are poor and lowly before God and who do his justice. They are told to seek three things: the LORD himself, righteousness, and humility.

The word perhaps is honest. It holds out hope without presuming on God. The humble who seek him here are the remnant who will be left in chapter 3.
passages.later: Amos gave the same call with the same perhaps: ‘Perhaps the LORD, the God of Hosts, will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph’ (Amos 5:15). Joel asked, ‘Who knows? He may turn and relent’ (Joel 2:14).
passages.asks: Zephaniah calls the humble to seek the LORD, righteousness and humility. Ask which of the three you most need to seek now. And ask what it would mean to hope in God's mercy without presuming on it.

passages.t: Philistia, Moab and Ammon, and Cush
passages.happening:
‘For Gaza will be abandoned, and Ashkelon left in ruins. Ashdod will be driven out at noon, and Ekron will be uprooted’ (verse 4). Woe to the people of the seacoast, the Cherethites, the land of the Philistines (verse 5). The coast will become pasture for shepherds and belong to the remnant of Judah, and God will restore their fortunes (verses 6-7).

God has heard the taunts of Moab and the insults of the Ammonites, who mocked his people and threatened their borders (verse 8). Moab will be like Sodom and Ammon like Gomorrah, a place of weeds and salt pits, and the remnant of God's people will take what was theirs (verse 9), in return for their pride (verse 10). The LORD will be terrifying to them, and ‘the nations of every shore will bow in worship to Him, each in its own place’ (verse 11). The Cushites too will fall by his sword (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
The Philistines lived on the southern coastal plain in five chief cities; four appear here. Gath, the fifth, had declined by this time and is also missing from Amos 1. The Cherethites were a people linked with the Philistines, often tied to Crete, and some served as David's bodyguard. Moab and Ammon lay east of the Jordan and the Dead Sea, and their hostility to Israel was old. The comparison with Sodom and Gomorrah was pointed, because Genesis traces both peoples to Lot, who had lived in Sodom. Weeds and salt pits describe the land around the Dead Sea, where salt made farming impossible.

Cush was the land south of Egypt, in what is now Sudan. Its kings had ruled Egypt until the middle of the seventh century BC, so the Cushites may stand for Egypt.

The judgments circle Judah, west, east, south and north. Verse 11 breaks out of the pattern: the gods of the earth are starved, and the nations bow to the LORD, each in its own place.
passages.later: Genesis traces Moab and Ammon to Lot (Genesis 19:37-38). Amos also named Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon and Ekron, without Gath (Amos 1:6-8).
passages.hard:
Does the promise that Judah's remnant will take the lands of other nations endorse conquest?

Verses 7 and 9 promise that the remnant of Judah will pasture on the Philistine coast and take what Moab and Ammon held, and modern readers can hear this as a charter for conquest. Several points help. The oracles describe God's judgment on particular nations for particular acts, taunting, threatening borders and pride, and the reversal is presented as God's justice for a people who had been victims, not as a mandate for later generations to seize land. The picture is poetic, using images of pasture, flocks and restored captives. And verse 11 at once widens the view to the nations worshiping the LORD; the book's last chapter promises that the peoples will call on his name with pure lips.

Interpreters differ on how literally to read the land promises. They give no warrant for violence against any people, and they make no claim about any modern state or border.
passages.asks: Moab and Ammon mocked God's people when they were weak. Ask whether you have ever taunted someone in their weakness. And verse 11 pictures every nation bowing to God in its own place. Ask how that picture changes the way you see other peoples.

passages.happening:
God will stretch out his hand against the north and destroy Assyria. ‘He will make Nineveh a desolation, as dry as a desert’ (verse 13). Flocks and wild creatures will lie down in her, and owls will roost on her pillars (verse 14).

This was the carefree city that lived securely and said to herself that she was the one, and there was no one besides her. Now she is a ruin, a resting place for animals, and everyone who passes by hisses and shakes a fist (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
Nineveh, the capital of Assyria on the Tigris, was still standing when Zephaniah spoke. It fell to the Babylonians and Medes in 612 BC, which is why the book is dated before then.

The city's boast in verse 15 is a claim that belongs to God alone. In Isaiah, the LORD says that he is God and there is no other (Isaiah 45:5). Nineveh said it of herself. Pride that puts itself in God's place is the root of her fall.

The picture of a great city become a home for owls and flocks is the prophets' usual language for complete ruin. These notes do not gloat over it, and it is no key for reading any city's suffering today as deserved.
passages.later: Nahum gives a whole book to Nineveh's fall (Nahum 1:1). Isaiah gives Babylon the same boast: ‘I am, and there is none besides me’ (Isaiah 47:8).
passages.asks: Nineveh said there was no one besides her. Ask where you have lived as if you were the center of everything. And ask what it would mean to let God be God in your life.
